It warned of possible flu outbreaks at schools at the start of the new academic year, increasing the risk of community transmission. Respiratory medicine specialist Raymond Tso, also a council member of the association, said the city saw an increasing number of cases from late August to early September. “Always when the school students get together, there will be increased chances of influenza infection because they are getting into a close community,” he said. “That’s why we advise people to get their vaccination sooner to prevent any serious consequences of flu infections.” Infectious disease specialist Joseph Tsang said more than 2.03 million doses of seasonal flu vaccine were administered in the 2025-26 season – similar to the previous year. He said there was a rise in the vaccination uptake among children and adolescents, but the coverage among people aged 50 to 64 and pregnant women remained relatively low. records.content: 澎湃号·政务 > 【传染病防控小贴士】流感疫苗接种系列科普问答 浙江健康教育 浙江健康教育官方澎湃号 2026-09-09 10:36 浙江 1.流感和普通感冒有什么区别? 答:流感与普通感冒最大的区别是病原体不同。流感是由流感病毒感染引起的一种急性呼吸道传染病,呈季节性流行;而普通感冒可由鼻病毒等多种病原体引起,通常在受凉、气候突变、过度疲劳等情况下发生,免疫力低下时容易患病。 从典型症状上来看,流感除伴有咽喉痛、干咳、鼻塞、流涕等呼吸道症状外,还常有高热、寒战、头痛、肌肉关节酸痛、乏力等全身症状,严重时可以导致肺炎、心肌损伤、休克等并发症,部分人在感染流感后可发展为重症、危重症甚至死亡;普通感冒则主要是咽痛、流涕、鼻塞、咳嗽等呼吸道症状,较少出现全身症状,或仅有轻微乏力,很少出现严重并发症。 2.流感病毒全人群易感吗? 答:流感病毒易发生变异,人群普遍易感。60岁及以上老人、5岁以下儿童,以及患有基础性疾病的人群,是流感的高风险人群,感染后出现严重并发症的风险较高。 3.目前我国流行的流感病毒有哪些类型? 答:流感病毒可以分为甲(A)、乙(B)、丙(C)、丁(D)四个型别。当前在人群中传播流行的是甲型(H1N1亚型和H3N2亚型)和乙型流感病毒(Victoria系),三者会交替或叠加出现,形成每年的季节性流行。每年接种的流感疫苗针对季节性流感,包含了上述3个组分(甲型H1N1亚型、甲型H3N2亚型和乙型Victoria系)。 4.流感的高发季节是什么时候,不同季节的流感病毒有差异吗? 答:我国流感呈现季节性流行特征,每年秋季开始逐渐进入流感流行季,冬春季(每年11月至次年3月)是流感等呼吸道传染病的高发季节,流行高峰一般出现在12月中下旬至次年1月初。北方省份呈现明显的冬春季流行高峰,南方省份除了冬春季流行高峰,有时也会出现夏季流行。 不同季节、不同年份流行的流感病毒存在差异。目前引起季节性流行的主要是甲型流感病毒的H1N1和H3N2亚型,以及乙型流感病毒的Victoria系。不同流行季的优势毒株有所不同,即使在同一流行季内,不同型别和亚型的流感病毒也可能交替成为优势毒株。 5.不同流行季的流感疫苗,组分上有什么变化? 答:全球使用的流感疫苗株,是每年由世界卫生组织基于全球流感监测数据,进行更新推荐的。与上一年度相比,本年度三种疫苗组分均有更新。世界卫生组织推荐的2026—2027年度北半球基于鸡胚生产的三价流感疫苗组分为: • A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus • A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus • B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus 6.为什么每年都需要接种流感疫苗? 答:接种流感疫苗是防控流感最经济有效的手段,需要每年接种的原因,一是流感病毒变异频繁,世界卫生组织每年推荐流感疫苗株,不同年度流感疫苗针对的流感病毒株可能有所不同。 二是流感疫苗接种后,产生的保护性抗体水平,随时间推移而逐渐衰减。接种流感疫苗后的保护作用,一般可维持6—8个月。即使流感病毒未发生较大变异,上一年度接种流感疫苗的保护效果也会降低。 7.哪些人群属于建议优先接种流感疫苗的人群? 答:建议6月龄及以上且没有接种禁忌的人员,每年接种流感疫苗。以下人员建议优先接种:第一类是感染流感后出现重症风险高的人群,包括≥60岁的老年人、慢性病患者、6月龄—5岁的儿童,养老机构、长期护理机构、福利院的居住人员等,这类人群感染流感病毒以后,容易并发肺炎等并发症,而且还有加重原有基础性疾病的可能。 第二类是感染风险高的人群,包括托幼机构和中小学校学生、医务人员等,上述人群由于所处环境人口密度相对高、职业暴露等,感染流感的风险、出现聚集性疫情的风险较高,接种流感疫苗以后,不仅能够预防自身的感染,还可以保护身边感染后容易出现重症的人群。 8.接种流感疫苗后多久能产生保护效果,建议何时接种流感疫苗? 答:接种流感疫苗不是“打完马上就有保护”,通常接种后需要2—4周才能产生具有保护水平的抗体。因此,为了获得较好的保护,建议在流行季来临前完成接种。综合我国流感流行特点,建议每年在9—10月完成接种,即使此时间段内未完成接种,整个流行季期间任何时候都可以接种。尤其是对于“一老一小”、慢性病患者等流感重症风险人群,接种疫苗可为后续潜在的感染风险提供免疫保护。 9.接种流感疫苗后需要在接种门诊留观多久,需要注意什么? 答:接种疫苗后需要按照规定在接种门诊现场留观30分钟,无异常后方可离开。回家后也应保持接种局部皮肤的清洁和干燥,避免用手抓挠接种部位;注意观察有无异常状况,必要时可向接种单位或疾控机构等进行咨询或报告,并根据情况及时就医。 10.曾经得过流感,还需要接种流感疫苗吗? 答:同一个流感流行季中,可能会有两种及以上的不同病毒型别或亚型共同或交替流行,不同亚型之间缺乏有效的交叉保护,因此感染过其中一种后,仍可能再感染其他类型的流感病毒。即使曾经得过流感,仍建议在符合接种条件的情况下,接种当前流行季流感疫苗,以降低再次感染其他型别或亚型流感病毒,以及发生并发症和重症的风险。如果正处于发热、急性发病或慢性病急性发作期,可待痊愈或病情稳定后再接种。 来 源 | 国家疾控局 编 辑 | 任少凡 声 明 | 资料来源网络,且仅用于科普公益宣传,如侵删。/健康科普 原标题:《【传染病防控小贴士】流感疫苗接种系列科普问答》 阅读原文 特别声明 本文为澎湃号作者或机构在澎湃新闻上传并发布,仅代表该作者或机构观点,不代表澎湃新闻的观点或立场,澎湃新闻仅提供信息发布平台。申请澎湃号请用电脑访问https://renzheng.thepaper.cn。 相关推荐 iPhone 18 Pro系列多电商平台售罄 蓝鲸新闻 15小时前 上海职工医保个人账户明起可支付116款二类疫苗,包含流感、狂犬疫苗等 10%公司 18小时前 科普 | 耳朵痒就要掏?别把“天然护盾”当垃圾 说医说 4天前 科普 | 开学季,这些“小动作”家长老师都要盯紧 说医说 4天前 24小时最热 游客在距离市区约30公里的泸州东站下车后建议更改站名,官方答复 中国政库 21小时前 596评 01:07 “泸州东”不在泸州市区?你还遇到过哪些“名在市、站在县”的高铁站 锋线视频 9小时前 43评 超30家药企长期行贿,涉案1.84亿!河北医科大学第二医院回应:正配合监管部门开展工作 10%公司 19小时前 197评 十大券商看后市|A股短期胜率和赔率均提升,保持信心和冷静 牛市点线面 23小时前 40评 外交部:散播人工智能威胁叙事不符合任何一方利益 大国外交 15小时前 62评 你有权知道更多 下载澎湃新闻客户端 下载APP A股持续震荡,韧性从何而来?五大券商首席发声:多重积极因素已形成支撑 王毅同法国外长巴罗通电话 敬一丹账号发布生平回顾视频 特朗普“嘴炮”要成真?苏威北爱三地领导人聚首,商讨抱团“脱英”

records.content: Conditions & Care Navigating Respiratory Season: Your Complete Guide To COVID, Flu And RSV Vaccines By Dr. Diana Rangaves, PharmD • Sep 9, 2026 Medically Reviewed by Dr. Justus Rabach, MD (Gustavo Fring/Pexels) Getting ready for the fall and winter respiratory virus season can raise questions about immunizations you might need, when to get them and how to keep your family safe. As part of a coordinated effort, the leading national medical groups issued joint respiratory immunization guidance for the 2026-2027 season in September 2026, in the wake of administrative changes and litigation against the federal Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), The Hill reports. The coalition, which includes the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), based their joint guidelines on a detailed scientific review published in JAMA, in partnership with the American Medical Association (AMA) and the Vaccine Integrity Project at the University of Minnesota. The best way to prevent severe illness, hospitalization and death from the “tripledemic” threats of influenza, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is through comprehensive protection. Federal advisory groups are considering legal and administrative changes, but practicing clinicians strongly recommend adherence to evidence-based medical consensus. Knowing how these vaccines work, which ones are suitable for you and your family, and how to schedule them in time means your family will remain healthy as the weather cools down. Can you get COVID and RSV at the same time? Yes, it is possible to have simultaneous infections with both COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a clinical condition known as viral coinfection, UC Health Today notes. Both pathogens attack the respiratory mucosal lining and are circulating during the overlapping late fall and winter seasons, meaning that exposure to one does not confer immunity to the other. If multiple different viruses invade the respiratory system at the same time, the physiological load can be much worse. According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), co-infection often increases inflammation in the local airways, overwhelms the alveoli’s ability to exchange gases and exhausts the defense mechanisms of the mucous membranes. Dr. Justus Rabach, MD , tells Blavity Health, “The combination of these two viruses is especially harmful for infants, young toddlers and older adults with cardiopulmonary conditions, and significantly increases the risk of severe bronchiolitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), bacterial pneumonia and intensive care admissions.” Vaccine 1: Seasonal Influenza (Flu) Influenza vaccination remains the single most important component of fall preventive health care, and the influenza A and B strains that circulate each winter continue to change rapidly, NIH explains. Based on the revised consensus recommendations published in JAMA, the medical coalition recommends that everyone 6 months of age and older receive a flu vaccine every flu season. A two-dose series, four weeks apart, is needed for children ages 6 months to 8 years receiving the flu shot for the first time to establish baseline antibody protection. All persons 6 months of age and older should be vaccinated against the flu each flu season, including special formulations for higher-risk groups among adults. High-dose, adjuvanted, and recombinant influenza vaccines, as well as newer mRNA vaccines approved for influenza, are all highly recommended for adults aged 65+, as they are more likely to elicit a strong humoral immune response in aging immune systems. A pregnant woman should get an inactive flu shot at any stage of her pregnancy, as this can not only protect her from serious lung complications, but also pass immunity to the baby through the placenta, as well as boost the baby’s immune system for its first six months of life. Vaccine 2: Updated COVID-19 While SARS-CoV-2 continues to evolve antigenically, new COVID-19 formulations are designed to target the most recent circulating subvariant and ensure robust levels of neutralizing antibodies each year. The unified medical guidelines have established a well-defined age-stratified approach to the care of children and adolescents: Infants and toddlers aged 6-23 months should receive the revised COVID-19 vaccine series. Epidemiological data also show that under two years of age, infants are at a similar or greater risk of being hospitalized as elderly adults 65 years of age or older because of their completely naive immune systems and small airway diameters. The coalition recommends vaccinating children and adolescents aged 2 to 18 years who are at higher risk for certain clinical conditions, such as obesity, congenital heart defects, asthma, diabetes, immunosuppressive conditions, and other clinical conditions, as well as those who are vaccinated due to family preference (shared clinical decision making). All adults should get the updated COVID-19 vaccine every year, especially those aged 50 and older, those living in long-term care settings, and immunocompromised people, who continue to be at higher risk of serious lower respiratory illness and post-acute sequelae of COVID-19. Vaccine 3: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) RSV is a seasonal virus that commonly causes cold-like illness in healthy adults, but is the number one cause of infant hospitalizations and one of the most important causes of severe pneumonia in older adults. The medical guidelines state that nirsevimab, a long-acting monoclonal antibody vaccine, should be given to all infants aged 8 months and under, shortly before or in the first RSV season of the baby’s life, if the mother had not been given the maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy. A dose is recommended for young children between 8 and 19 months old who are entering their second RSV season and who are considered to be at high risk for RSV from chronic lung disease of prematurity, severe cystic fibrosis or congenital heart anomaly. Mothers who are expecting can also directly protect their newborns by getting vaccinated against RSV during pregnancy with the maternal RSV bivalent vaccine (Abrysvo) between 32 and 36 weeks, which boosts maternal antibodies that are transferred to the fetus. The medical coalition advises giving the RSV vaccine once in life to all adults aged 75 and older. Also, adults aged 50 to 74 years should get the vaccine once if they have chronic heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), end-stage renal disease or severe diabetes . Best practices Multiple seasonal shots may seem like a logistical hassle, but evidence-based clinical practices help get the most protection. The Mayo Clinic states that timing is an important factor in vaccine effectiveness. Late September and October are the best times to get the influenza and COVID-19 vaccines. Vaccination during this fall window allows for the number of neutralizing antibodies to peak at the same time as the peak of community viral transmission, which is between December and February. It is safe and very effective to administer several vaccines at a single clinical visit (coadministration). Getting your flu shot and COVID-19 vaccine at the same time won’t diminish the immune response to either vaccine. When two shots are given at the same time, the healthcare provider will use a different arm, or the injection sites will be at least 1 inch apart on the same arm, so it is easier to see if there is any discomfort at the injection site. Clinicians recommend delaying routine vaccinations if patients have acute moderate or severe disease with a high fever, to prevent an acute vaccine reaction from being misinterpreted as disease progression. If you are suffering from mild congestion or low-grade sniffles, it shouldn’t put off your visit. Moreover, having recently recovered from a diagnosed COVID-19 infection, you can wait about three months for your next COVID-19 booster, as natural infection provides strong, temporary mucosal immunity. Bottom line Immunization recommendations for the 2026–2027 respiratory season from key medical groups offer straightforward, evidence-based guidance for protecting people against influenza (the flu), COVID-19 and RSV. Flu vaccines for all over 6 months of age, COVID-19 vaccines by age and RSV vaccines for targeted groups of infants, pregnant people and high-risk older adults create a comprehensive defense against severe diseases during the season. Scheduling shots between late September and October will provide high antibody levels during the winter peak period and help protect vulnerable family members. Frequently Asked Questions Is it safe to get the RSV and flu vaccines at the same time? Yes, extensive clinical trial data show that it is safe to receive the RSV vaccine and seasonal flu shot during the same medical visit without diminishing the effectiveness of either immunization. What is the recommended gap between two vaccines? Most standard inactivated and mRNA respiratory vaccines do not require a waiting period between doses and can be given simultaneously; however, live attenuated vaccines must either be administered on the same day or spaced at least four weeks apart. What to expect after ‘superflu' winter As respiratory virus season approaches, experts discuss what we may expect this flu season and how to protect yourself. By Caroline Kee | TODAY • Published September 9, 2026 • Updated on September 9, 2026 at 1:58 pm BOOKMARKER Summer isn’t officially over yet, but respiratory viruses are already beginning to ramp up across the United States. Seasonal influenza activity is still low compared to COVID-19, but experts are already urging people to prepare for flu season. Last winter, the country faced an unprecedented, severe flu epidemic fueled by the highly mutated H3N2 subclade K flu variant, dubbed the “super flu.” Watch NBC 4 free wherever you are WATCH HERE It was one of the worst flu seasons in decades, and doctors’ visits for flu-like illness reached the highest levels seen in over 25 years, according to data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Earlier this year, scientists updated the 2026-2027 flu shots to protect against the subclade K strain. As vaccines are rolled out, you may be wondering what to expect in the coming months. In the U.S., flu activity typically peaks between December and February, per the CDC. But the timing and severity of flu seasons can vary from year to year. Are there any signs that the flu virus could mutate again this fall? Could we be in for another severe flu season, and how can you protect yourself? TODAY.com spoke to experts to find out. How bad will the 2026-2027 flu season be? “The only thing that’s predictable about influenza is it’s unpredictable,” Dr. Daniel Jernigan, a former CDC director and a contributing scholar at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. It’s still too early to tell how the 2026-2027 flu season will unfold, but there are some early clues, experts say. Predicting the severity of flu seasons is a delicate art, Dr. Albert Ko, professor of epidemiology at Yale School of Public Health, tells TODAY.com. Scientists use a combination of forecasting models and look at trends in the Southern hemisphere, which experiences its winter and flu season earlier in the year. Australia is often viewed as a harbinger for what to expect stateside. Australia’s 2026 flu season has been moderate so far, and much milder compared to last season — the country’s busiest and deadliest in decades, says Ko. Data shows cases are surging later than usual, but are nowhere near the peak in 2025. “I wouldn’t sound the warning signs about what’s happening in Australia now,” says Ko. However, flu activity in the Southern hemisphere isn’t always a reliable indicator, and sometimes the U.S. trends don’t follow. “It’s not linear,” Jernigan adds. It’s also rare to see two severe flu seasons back-to-back, but that’s exactly what happened last winter. The 2024-2025 flu season was considered “high severity,” per the CDC, and it was followed by another record-breaking season last winter. “I did not expect the big season last year because we just had a bad season. ... It flummoxed most of us who follow flu closely,” Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist and professor of medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells TODAY.com. While there are some early signs to suggest we’re in for a milder flu season, “always prepare for the worst,” Schaffner says. Cold and flu season is on the way, and some of the leading U.S. medical groups are offering their own guidance on vaccinations. Is there a new flu variant? So far, there is no evidence that a new, mutated flu variant will drive cases this flu season, the experts say. There are two main types of influenza that cause seasonal epidemics: influenza A (H3N2 and H1N1) and influenza B. Last winter’s flu surge, as well as the Southern hemisphere’s 2026 flu season, was fueled largely by H3N2 subclade K. The highly contagious variant emerged early last year, and has seven mutations that caused it to “drift” from the H3N2 strain in the flu shot. “We’re always worried about antigenic shifts, or changes in those viruses because that can set off larger and expected seasonal waves of of influenza,” says Ko. So far, there’s no evidence that the flu virus has picked up significant mutations that set it apart from the strains circulating, including H3N2 subclade K, according to the experts. But experts remain cautious because the influenza virus mutates constantly. “The virus is in control ... and until you actually go through it, you’re never 100% certain,” Dr. Ronald Nahass, president of the Infectious Disease Society of America, tells TODAY.com. A significant portion of the U.S. population still has not been exposed to subclade K and may be at risk, Jernigan notes, adding “we’re (still) closely watching subclade K.” Flu symptoms The flu isn’t a mild cold. The symptoms are intense and start suddenly — what many experts describe as feeling like “being hit by a truck.” The most common signs of flu infection include: Severe fatigue Fever Chills Body aches Runny or stuffy nose Sore throat Cough Less commonly, the flu may cause diarrhea and vomiting, which is more common among children than adults, per the CDC. Most healthy people will recover from flu on their own, but it can cause you to feel miserable for up to two weeks. Adults over the age of 65, children under 5, pregnant women and immunocompromised people are at higher risk for severe disease or complications from the flu, says Schaffner. However, the flu can become deadly for anyone. If you develop severe flu symptoms or you’re in a high-risk group, contact your healthcare provider, says Schaffner. It’s cold and flu season again, which means you could be left wondering which virus is causing your symptoms. Here’s what you need to know. Flu tests and treatments The only way to know if you have the flu is to get tested. The experts recommend stocking up on 3-in-1 rapid home tests for influenza A, influenza B and COVID-19 ahead of the fall. If you test positive, there are treatment options available. Antiviral drugs help the body fight the flu virus, which can help lessen symptoms and shorten the duration of illness by a day or two, per the CDC. Flu treatment is most important for people who develop severe symptoms or are in a high-risk group, the experts note. Flu antivirals require a positive flu test and a prescription from a doctor, and work best when started within one to two days after you start feeling sick, the experts note. Are the new flu shots available? Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself from the flu, the experts emphasize. The influenza vaccine reduces the risk of severe disease, complications and death. It’s not 100% effective. “You can get flu vaccine and still get the flu. That does not mean that the vaccine has failed. It’s designed to keep you out of the hospital, out of the intensive care unit, and out of the cemetery,” Schaffner adds. The 2026-2027 flu vaccines are available and being rolled out at pharmacies, doctor’s offices and hospitals across the country. The shots are trivalent, per the CDC, which means they protect against three viruses: influenza A H1N1 (pdm09), influenza A H3N2, and influenza B (Victoria lineage). There are multiple vaccine options available this year. These include standard egg-based flu shots, high-dose shots, cell-based shots and a nasal mist. Last month, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a new mRNA flu vaccine from Moderna for adults ages 50 and older. The mRNA flu vaccine was shown to be about 27% more effective than standard flu shots in a trial, NBC News reported. These are safe, and the mRNA technology is very promising, Nahass notes. Although the mRNA shots are expected to be available this fall, supply will likely be limited, Schaffner notes. “I encourage people to talk to their physicians about which vaccine they should get. There are lots of choices,” says Nahass. 2026-2027 flu shot guidelines The CDC usually makes an official federal recommendation for flu vaccines every September. This guides providers, patients, and insurers. However, the expert panel in charge of this decision, the Advisory Committee for Immunization Practices (ACIP), was sidelined earlier this year. Instead, the CDC stated that its guidance from 2025 would remain in effect for the 2026-2027 season — which creates confusion, experts say. In lieu of new guidelines, leading medical groups came together with the Vaccine Integrity Project to issue a joint vaccine recommendation ahead of respiratory virus season. These include the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Medicine, American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology and the Infectious Disease Society of America. “It’s our collaborative effort to fill the void by the CDC and the ACIP, which didn’t provide up-to-date guidance regarding respiratory vaccines,” says Nahass. The groups strongly recommended that everyone ages 6 months and older (including pregnant women) get an annual flu vaccine, and people who are ages 65 or older or have weakened immune systems get a high-dose flu shot. These guidelines were based on evidence published in JAMA showing the flu vaccine protects against severe disease and cuts the risk of hospitalization, especially for high-risk groups. “Since the risks of the vaccine are so low and the benefits are so great, the medical community has come down strongly to recommend that folks get vaccinated,” says Nahass. If you have questions, talk to your doctor. When is the best time to get a flu shot? The best time to get a flu shot is late September or October, experts say. “We want the protection to extend throughout the winter, beyond February into March. That’s a pretty long reach, and so you don’t want to get the flu vaccine too early,” says Schaffner. It takes about two weeks for the body to respond and the flu shot to take full effect, and this protection lasts around six months. While it’s never “too late” to get a flu shot, the experts encourage people not to wait until flu activity is spiking. “It’s not as useful once we’re in the wave. You’re going to get most bang for the buck by getting the flu shot earlier,” says Ko. Similarly, the experts urge parents to vaccinate their children before the flu is sweeping through schools. “There are children who die each year of influenza. It’s a great tragedy. The vast majority of them are unvaccinated, but about half of the children who die are healthy,” says Schaffner. How to protect against flu If you’re concerned about the flu, your best bet is getting the flu shot. Vaccination is the most effective way to protect yourself, but you can take extra tried-and-true actions to fight the spread of respiratory viruses, Schaffner notes. Here are some more tips going into flu season: Wear a well-fitted N95 or mask in crowded settings. Wash your hands frequently. Test if you have symptoms. Contact your healthcare provider if you get sick. Cover coughs and sneezes. Avoid contact with sick people. “Listen to your doctors,” says Nahass. This story first appeared on TODAY.com. records.content_title: Flu Cases Surge in Shanghai and Hangzhou as Schools Report Classwide Isolation
records.content: Multiple classes across Shanghai are sent home for isolation, with some classes shut down entirely. One Shanghai parent posts on social media asking: "What's going on with the flu in Shanghai?" (Screenshot via NTD) Flu cases are climbing sharply across Shanghai and Hangzhou just as the new school semester gets underway, prompting a wave of classwide quarantines and school closures across the two cities' primary schools and kindergartens. The Chinese regime’s state-run and local government-affiliated outlets—including Hangzhou News and Nanjing Morning Post—along with individual Weibo users, have published multiple accounts describing crowded pediatric wards, sudden school notices, and families scrambling to keep up as the outbreak spreads through classrooms in both cities. The disruption has hit families within days of the semester starting. In Hangzhou, the capital city of China's east coastal Zhejiang Province, one mother said her third-grade daughter's teacher sent a text just a week into the term. “10 of the roughly 40 students in the class had already gone home with fevers, and about half tested positive for flu,” Li said, cited by Hangzhou News Center. Her daughter is a year-3 primary pupil who was not affected by the flu. Li said that, under local health authority requirements, the entire class was ordered to quarantine at home for four days, from Sept. 11 to Sept. 14, before returning to school Sept. 15. Parents describe similar scenes playing out across Shanghai, one of China's major financial hubs roughly 120 miles northeast of Hangzhou. One parent wrote on social media: "What's going on with the flu in Shanghai? We got a notice first thing in the morning that the whole class was quarantined, and by afternoon we found out half the kids were out sick," according to a report by Nanjing Morning Post on Sept. 14. The publication in Nanjing reported another case of quarantine in Shanghai: one flu case, a four-day shutdown for the whole class. According to the publication, at 4:41 p.m. on Sept. 2, a parent in Baoshan, a northern suburb of Shanghai, received a notice in a group chat from the head teacher: "We’ve had one case of seasonal flu confirmed in the class. Per requirements from the local health authority, Class Da Yi (equivalent to Pre-K in the U.S. system) will undergo a four-day quarantine period, from Sept. 2 to Sept. 5. Kids can come back to class as normal on Sept. 7." A blogger by the name Tingxintang also posted this case on China’s digital mouthpiece NetEase, adding that, with less than two weeks into the new semester, multiple classes across Shanghai had been sent home for isolation one after another, with some schools shutting down entirely. China's National Disease Control and Prevention Administration (NDCPA) addressed the outbreak of the flu, claiming that the strains currently circulating nationally are influenza A (subtypes H1N1 and H3N2) and influenza B (Victoria lineage), which tend to circulate in alternation or overlap to produce each year's seasonal wave. A Third of Hospital Beds Now Occupied by Kids Infected with Flu: Doctor Dr. Qi Zhenghong, chief physician of the infectious disease department at Hangzhou Children's Hospital, said flu-related outpatient visits and hospital admissions among children have risen sharply since the semester began, according to Hangzhou News Center. "Before this, we just had a handful of flu patients in the ward here and there," Qi said. "Now flu cases make up about a third of our hospital beds, with roughly 10 kids admitted every single day." Qi said this season's dominant strain is influenza A H3N2, mixed in with influenza B's Victoria strain, and that kids in kindergarten and the early grades of elementary school are getting hit the hardest. She's also seeing a clear pattern: once one person in a household gets sick, the whole family tends to go down one by one. In one case, a grandmother came down with the flu first and passed it to her 3-year-old grandson, who ran a high fever for days and had it worse than the adults did. Not long after, both parents got sick too. Qi said many household outbreaks followed the same pattern: an adult picked up the virus outside, brought it home, and passed it to a kid with a weaker immune system, who later spread it to the whole family. "Kids also tend to stay sick longer than adults do, which makes it that much easier for the flu to spread through an entire household," Qi said. The NDCPA said China's flu season typically runs from autumn through winter and early spring, entering its high-transmission period between November and March, with the seasonal peak usually landing in mid-to-late December through early January. Northern provinces see a clear winter-spring peak, while southern provinces—in addition to that same winter-spring peak—sometimes also experience a secondary summer wave of flu activity. The blogger Tingxintang shared a Shanghai parent's question: "Is the flu hitting Shanghai earlier than usual this year?" Conversation Conversations are moderated. records.content: 流感疫苗四价转三价,政策红利能否打开市场空间? 21新健康韩利明 2026-09-10 19:40 允许职工医保个人账户支付在定点医疗机构发生的流感疫苗费用 21世纪经济报道记者 韩利明 每年9月至次年5月,是我国流感病毒流行的高发期。时值金秋开学季,流感疫苗接种进入关键窗口期。 日前,在国家疾控局举行的新闻发布会上,中日友好医院呼吸与危重症医学科主任医师曹彬指出,每一个流感季,常见的流行毒株是有差异的,目前流行的主要是两种甲型流感和一种乙型流感,甲型流感是H1N1(简称甲1)、H3N2(简称甲3),乙型流感现在比较流行的是Victoria系的流感病毒。 “不同的流感流行季,推荐流感疫苗的组分也是不一样的,流感疫苗株是世界卫生组织根据全球流感监测的主要流行亚型来推荐的。因此,每年推荐的流感疫苗株也是有所差别的。所以说,需要大家能够充分理解,并每年适时接种今年适用的流感疫苗。”曹彬强调。 结合中国疾病预防控制中心9月2日发布的《中国流感疫苗预防接种技术指南(2026—2027)》(下称《指南》),2026年流感疫苗最大的变化是“四价转三价”。这并非疫苗“减配”,而是基于病毒流行趋势的科学调整。 本次调整系因世界卫生组织监测发现,乙型Yamagata系毒株自2020年3月后已无主流传播风险,2026年—2027年流感季全球统一推荐使用三价流感疫苗,不再纳入该毒株组分。更新后的三价疫苗精准覆盖WHO预判的当前流行的甲型H1N1、H3N2和乙型Victoria系毒株。 建议在9—10月完成接种 国家流感中心最新监测数据显示,截至2026年8月30日当周,南方省份流感病毒检测阳性率上升、北方省份流感活动水平低,全国A(H3N2)占比升高。全国未报告流感样病例暴发疫情。 不过《指南》提醒,通常接种流感疫苗2—4周后,可产生具有保护水平的抗体。综合我国南、北方的流感流行特点,通常在11月份左右进入冬春季流感流行季,建议在9—10月完成接种;即使此时间段内未完成接种,整个流行季也都可以接种。 《指南》建议所有6月龄及以上且无接种禁忌的人接种流感疫苗,且优先推荐以下重点和高风险人群接种,包括医务人员、60岁及以上的老年人、罹患一种或多种慢性病者、养老机构及福利院等人群聚集场所脆弱人群及员工、6月龄—5岁儿童、托幼机构及中小学校等重点场所人群等。 疫苗品类方面,《指南》推荐三价流感疫苗,包括三价灭活疫苗(IIV3)和三价减毒活疫苗(LAIV3)。其中IIV3有裂解疫苗和亚单位疫苗,可用于6月龄及以上人群;LAIV3适用于3—17岁人群。 21世纪经济报道记者注意到,近期多地医院及社区卫生服务中心开放疫苗接种预约,价格各异。例如永胜县中医医院引入3款流感疫苗,疫苗价格分别为63元/剂、98元/剂、308元/剂,另收取15元/剂接种服务费。 根据相关报道,成都市成华区青龙社区卫生服务中心最近一周流感疫苗接种量约600至700人次;三价裂解灭活疫苗(6月龄及以上适用)75元/剂,已包含接种服务费;3—17岁适用鼻喷三价减毒活疫苗328元/剂(含服务费)。 南京市玄武门社区卫生服务中心公示信息显示,华兰流感裂解疫苗6—35月龄儿童接种2剂,价格为68元/剂;3岁及以上人群单剂接种,单价88元/剂。江苏中慧元通流感亚单位疫苗6—35月龄人群接种2剂;3岁及以上人群单剂,疫苗价格298元/剂。 批签发节奏分化,政策红利有望打开增长空间 从疫苗产业供给端看,西南证券研报此前有数据显示,流感疫苗主要包括三价流感疫苗、亚单位疫苗、四价流感疫苗和冻干鼻喷流感疫苗。2026年上半年流感疫苗批签发9批次,同比下滑93%。其中,三价流感疫苗批签发5批次;亚单位疫苗和四价流感疫苗获批签发均为2批次。 其中,三价流感疫苗获批签发5批次,同比下滑89%,全部来自于科兴生物;亚单位流感疫苗获批签发2批次,同比下滑50%,全部来自于中慧元通;四价流感疫苗批签发2批次,同比下滑97%,全部来自于科兴生物;鼻喷流感疫苗上半年未获批签发,从竞争格局看,鼻喷流感疫苗全部来自百克生物。 21世纪经济报道记者初步统计,今年6月底至今,国内流感疫苗累计批签发49批次。市场观察人士指出,经历前几年价格战后,国内流感疫苗市场份额持续向头部企业集中。 回溯2024年,国内流感疫苗龙头华兰疫苗下调四价流感疫苗产品价格,核心产品降价幅度约30%。2025年其流感疫苗业务营收11.21亿元,同比增长4.43%,业务呈现回暖,但受价格战余波影响,板块毛利率同比下降2.77%。 2026年上半年,受行业整体批签发周期节奏影响,华兰疫苗暂无流感疫苗新批次完成批签发与销售,相关板块营收同比下滑。不过截至2026年8月,该公司共取得流感疫苗批签发16批次。 鼻喷赛道方面,百克生物感雾®是国内首款鼻腔喷雾给药的流感减毒活疫苗,其液体剂型鼻喷流感疫苗于7月获得批签发、8月初启动上市销售,丰富了国内儿童青少年的接种选择。 整体来看,目前我国流感疫苗总体接种率约3%,远低于欧美接近50%的接种率。同时,WHO提出老人、小孩、慢病患者等重点人群流感疫苗接种率要达到75%的目标,目前国内重点人群覆盖率还不足5%。业内预期,随着政策积极推动、公众接种意识提升,接种率将不断提升,流感疫苗市场增长空间广阔。 政策层面利好持续释放。2026年5月,国家医保局办公室首次明确,允许职工医保个人账户支付在定点医疗机构发生的流感疫苗费用;2026年7月,国务院印发《国民健康“十五五”规划》,提出推动二级及以上医疗机构提供预防接种服务,推行疫苗处方政策。 有业内人士向21世纪经济报道记者表示,长远来看,疫苗行业属于品种为王、技术驱动的赛道,伴随流感疫苗技术迭代、鼻喷等新型疫苗普及,以及全民防疫认知提升、配套接种政策落地,具备技术创新能力、完善的产品矩阵和渠道覆盖优势的头部企业,将持续抢占市场份额,引领行业高质量扩容。 (作者:韩利明 编辑:季媛媛,张明艳) records.content: Fort Worth, September 10 , 2026 | 09:01 AM America/Chicago Off the Sidelines: Why This Year’s Flu Vaccine Is a Game-Changer for Kids Marc Mazade, M.D. Written by Marc Mazade, M.D., MPH, m edical director of Infection Control and Prevention at Cook Children's My high school basketball coach insisted that we get a flu vaccine every year. He knew that flu is much more than just a cold. Flu is like getting hit by a train. He knew that recovery could take a couple of weeks. Flu vaccines might make you feel bad for a day, but feeling bad is a sign that our immune systems are working. That’s much better than getting knocked out of the game, missing a week of band competition, missing the big trip, or staying in bed while others exchange holiday gifts and treats. Flu season can run from November to May, so getting the flu vaccine in fall provides the longest protection from flu. During the last flu season, nearly 6,000 kids came to the emergency department and nearly 600 kids were hospitalized with flu at Cook Children’s Medical Center in Fort Worth (some would say an average season). Keeping folks out of the hospital is the main benefit of getting a flu vaccine, but not the only one. Because flu is passed between friends at school then spreads to family members, immunizing kids is key to controlling flu outbreaks. Closing hard-hit schools worsens hospital staff shortages as working parents must take off work to be with their kids, even when their kids aren’t sick. That can mean longer waiting times for patients and more shifts for exhausted health care workers. In 2025, the seasonal flu story got more interesting. An escape virus erupted onto the scene like a flash fire! Scientists found that “Subclade K” is a strain of influenza A (H3N2) that binds better to the membranes in our noses and is less sensitive to some antibodies (stuff that Infectious Diseases doctors love to chat about).1 Improved viral fitness means that chances are good that this escape virus will keep coming back until it is knocked off by a more fit flu strain. A big question last year was, “How effective are influenza vaccines going to be against the escape virus?” Thankfully, vaccine protection against hospitalization was pretty good, even among adults. But something extraordinary happened in kids who took the vaccine. While the vaccine protected adults against mild, moderate and severe flu only 32-39% of the time, kids were protected 70-79% of the time. It seems that children get more “bang for the buck” from influenza vaccine than adults. Also, for those who were not exposed to flu last year, this year’s influenza vaccines provide better protection against the escape virus. My coach made sure we got our flu shots because he didn’t want us watching from the sidelines. Years later, the science supports that same advice. Children receive remarkable protection from influenza vaccination, helping them avoid serious illness, stay out of the hospital and remain where they belong: in school, with their friends and families, and in the game. 1Al-Natour, L.M. 16 June 2026. Emerging Influenza A (H3N2) Subclade K: A narrative review. Natural Resources for Human Health, 6(3s). Pages 678-687. https://nrfhh.com/index.php/journal/article/view/522

records.content: Florida pharmacies and clinics are now offering updated flu and COVID vaccines for the 2026-27 respiratory illness season, though some may be harder to find. Floridians can expect to find the new Moderna mRNA flu shot, mFLUSIVA, at some of their local pharmacies in the next few weeks, but not all. “It started shipping out over the weekend (following FDA release of lots), so it should be available in stores imminently,” said Christopher Ridley, a Moderna spokesman. The new vaccine’s mRNA technology , the same platform as Moderna’s COVID shots, provides about 27% more coverage against influenza than traditional flu vaccines, according to a study of 40,000 adults ages 50-64. The technology allows it to be updated more quickly to match circulating virus strains. An mRNA vaccine is one that is lab-produced that teaches your body how to fight off an illness versus a standard vaccine, which is made by using a weakened live version of a virus. However, because Moderna missed the early contracting cycle for the standard U.S. flu vaccine rollout, you may have to hunt for it. Moderna said shipping to major pharmacies will scale up progressively throughout the fall. Moderna has created a Vaccine Finder to locate its flu and COVID vaccines by ZIP code. Most major pharmacies in Florida have not committed to carry Moderna’s mFLUSIVA this respiratory illness season. “We’ll continue to evaluate Moderna’s new vaccine, as we do with all our offerings, to ensure we continue to meet the needs of the communities we serve,” said CVS spokeswoman Roslyn Guarino. ” We are not offering the mRNA flu vaccine currently.” Publix spokeswoman Lindsey Willis said: “The mRNA flu vaccine is not yet available. Our Publix Pharmacy offers the standard vaccine, as well as one of the preferentially recommended vaccines for ages 65+.” Robin Edie, a Walmart spokesperson, said: “We do not currently offer the mFLUVISA vaccine, but customers can speak with their local Walmart pharmacist about recommended vaccinations.” Walmart pharmacies are giving out the traditional flu shots. Walgreens likely will be the first in Florida to offer mFLUSIVA. “Walgreens will offer the new mRNA flu vaccine in limited quantities this season. Availability will vary by location. Patients interested in receiving the vaccine are encouraged to speak with their local Walgreens pharmacist for more information,” a spokesperson said. The new mFLUSIVA vaccine is not made with eggs, giving people with egg allergies another option. Side effects reported during the trials included arm soreness, headache, chills, and temporary fatigue. Those occurred slightly more frequently with mFLUSIVA than with traditional flu shots. Traditional flu shots Medical groups are urging Americans to get vaccinated for the flu after two difficult respiratory seasons. Last year, the dominant strain differed from previous years, so Americans had less natural defense against it. “We did have a really, really stressful and tough flu season last year,” said Julie Caldwell, Walgreens senior manager of immunizations. “You can’t predict what’s going to happen from season to season, so the best advice is to get protected.” Experts agree that almost everyone starting at age 6 months benefits from a flu vaccine. However, flu is particularly concerning for people 65 and older, pregnant women, young children and people of any age who have chronic health problems. During the 2024-2025 flu season, about 45,000 people in the United States lost their lives. The seasonal influenza vaccines don’t block all flu infections, but they do help prevent hospitalizations, especially for those most at risk, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project , a public health group based at the University of Minnesota. On average, flu vaccines reduce the risk of needing to see a doctor by 30% to 60%, according to U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. This year’s traditional flu shots cover three seasonal flu strains, and five manufacturers offer them. If you are shot-averse, you can choose a nasal spray, FluMist, if you’re ages 2 to 49 and meet other health criteria. The CDC recommends three preferred types of high-dose shots for adults 65 and older: Fluad (Adjuvanted), Fluzone High-Dose, or Flublok (Recombinant). Studies show all three high-dose shots perform significantly better than standard-dose flu vaccines at preventing hospitalization and severe illness in older adults. The mRNA flu vaccine hasn’t been fully studied in the 65+ group. However, it was granted accelerated approval for that age group after producing a stronger immune response than traditional vaccines, with similar rates of severe side effects. Moderna is conducting more studies to see how it stacks up against existing high-dose vaccines for adults in that age range. Walgreens’ Caldwell says her pharmacies, for now, will recommend the higher dose of the traditional flu vaccine for customers 65 and older. “That’s the CDC recommendation as well for patients 65 plus,” she said. Dr. T’Anjuihsien Marx, MDNow’s regional medical director for North Broward and Palm Beach County, said his clinics already have begun giving flu shots to patients. “For now, we are sticking with traditional flu shots, the tried and true,” he said. When to get the flu shot Experts say late September or October are the best times to get vaccinated for influenza, which typically starts spreading in November. Flu vaccines typically take a few weeks to reach full protection. Marx said he prefers late mid- to late-October. “It’s a guessing game when the flu season is going to hit, but I feel like October gives a better chance to take you through the whole season, especially if we get a late surge in February or March,” he said. Youngvet via Getty Images Experts say late September or October are the best times to get vaccinated for influenza, which typically starts spreading in November. Flu vaccines typically take a few weeks to reach full protection. What to know about this year’s COVID shots This year, the FDA has formally approved COVID vaccines for higher-risk people — those ages 65 and older, or younger people with at least one health condition that increases their risk. However, medical groups recommend them for people 19 or older and say those 65 or older should get a second dose after six months. The fall COVID-19 vaccines have an updated formula targeting XFG, the dominant circulating strain. The Vaccine Integrity Project said last fall’s COVID-19 shots cut the risk of hospitalization by 53% in seniors and slashed emergency room visits for very young children. Depending on age, people can choose a COVID shot and seek a pharmacy that offers it. Four types of shots have been approved: Pfizer’s COMIRNATY COVID-19 vaccine for those 5 years and older. Moderna’s SPIKEVAX for those 6 months and older. Moderna’s mNEXSPIKE, a lower-dose Moderna shot approved for ages 12 and older. Novavax’s NUVAXOVID, a non-mRNA vaccine, for those 12 years and older. Not all pharmacies and clinics will carry the Novavax vaccine but the company does have a vaccine locator . Caldwell said Walgreens will offer all types, but the Novavax shot will be available only at certain locations. “People can go into our scheduler and select what they want or say no preference,” she said. Should you get an RSV vaccine? RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, typically is a cold-like nuisance during the fall, winter and early spring. But it can be severe, even life-threatening, for infants and older adults. RSV caused an estimated 2.8 million to 5.8 million outpatient visits, between 170,000 and 340,000 hospitalizations and as many as 25,000 deaths last year in the United States, according to the Vaccine Integrity Project. The American Academy of Family Physicians recommends a one-time vaccination for adults 75 and older, people 50 to 74 who are at increased risk, or younger people with weak immune systems. This season, there are three RSV vaccines: GSK, Pfizer, and Moderna. Caldwell said if you haven’t received the RSV vaccine, it’s just one dose, so consider getting that along with your COVID and flu shot in one visit. Cost and incentives Medicare covers the fall shots and most private health insurers say they plan to continue doing so through 2027. Most pharmacies take appointments or walk-ins. As an added benefit, several retailers are offering coupons with vaccinations. Patients who get a vaccine at Walgreens can earn $15 in Walgreens Cash rewards on their next in-store purchase of $5 or more as a myWalgreens® member. CVS offers a $5-off-$20 coupon after vaccination and Publix offers a $5 digital gift card after you receive your free flu shot. Walmart does not offer gift cards, cash bonuses, or rewards points for getting immunizations. South Florida Sun Sentinel health reporter Cindy Goodman can be reached at cgoodman@sunsentinel.com
